def: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: RL where a program (answer checker, unit tests, format check) computes the reward instead of a learned reward model.
A program that checks whether a model's output is correct, used as the reward in RLVR or to select among samples at inference time.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al., 2024): PPO-style RL that samples a group of responses per prompt and uses the group's mean and standard deviation of reward as the baseline, removing the critic network.
In GRPO, a response's reward minus its group's mean reward, usually divided by the group's standard deviation. Zero for every response when all rewards in the group are equal.
REINFORCE leave-one-out: each response's baseline is the mean reward of the other responses for the same prompt, giving an unbiased advantage estimate.
A GRPO variant (Liu et al., 2025) that drops per-response length normalisation and standard-deviation scaling to remove a length bias and a difficulty bias.
An RL recipe (Yu et al., 2025) adding clip-higher, dynamic sampling of informative groups, token-level loss, and overlong reward shaping to GRPO-style training.
Using a larger upper clipping bound than lower bound in the PPO ratio so low-probability tokens can be promoted faster, which helps preserve exploration.
The policy's output distribution becoming nearly deterministic during RL, so sampled responses stop differing and the learning signal disappears.
A prompt where every sampled response gets the same reward; it contributes no policy-gradient signal in group-baseline methods.
A small supervised fine-tuning stage on curated long chain-of-thought examples before reasoning RL, used in DeepSeek-R1 to improve readability and stability.
A reward model that scores each intermediate reasoning step rather than only the final answer.
A reward model, or verifier, that scores only the final result of a full response.
The per-sample estimator r − log r − 1, with r = π_ref/π_θ, used in GRPO. It is unbiased for KL(π_θ‖π_ref) and never negative.
A divisor applied to logits before softmax. Below 1 sharpens the distribution toward the top token; above 1 flattens it.
Sampling only from the k most probable next tokens.
Sampling from the smallest set of most probable tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p (Holtzman et al., 2020).
Keeping only tokens whose probability is at least a fraction p_min of the top token's probability, so the cutoff adapts to model confidence.
Always choosing the single most probable next token; deterministic.
The probability that at least one of k sampled responses is correct, estimated without bias from n ≥ k samples as 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k).
Sample k responses and return the most common final answer (Wang et al., 2022).
Generate N responses and return the one a reward model or verifier scores highest.
Extra computation spent when answering, such as longer reasoning, more samples, or search, to improve accuracy without retraining.
Stored attention keys and values for every previous token, reused at each decoding step; its size grows with layers, KV heads, context length, and concurrent sequences.
Attention in which several query heads share each key/value head, shrinking the KV cache.
Processing the input prompt in parallel before generation; usually compute-bound.
Generating output tokens one at a time; usually memory-bandwidth-bound.
A serving technique that adds new requests to a running batch as others finish, keeping accelerators busy.
A small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, producing the same output distribution faster (Leviathan et al., 2023).
Storing weights, and sometimes activations or the KV cache, in fewer bits (for example 8 or 4) to cut memory and raise speed, with some accuracy risk.
A post-training weight quantization method that uses approximate second-order information to minimise layer output error (Frantar et al., 2023).
Activation-aware weight quantization: protects the weights most important to activations when quantizing to low bit widths (Lin et al., 2024).
Refusing a benign request, often because it superficially resembles a harmful one. The false positive of safety behaviour.
Answering a genuinely harmful request. The false negative of safety behaviour.
Training with a written set of principles: the model critiques and revises its own outputs, and AI-generated preference labels replace human harmlessness labels (Bai et al., 2022).
Reinforcement learning from AI feedback: preference labels come from a model rather than from human raters.
Deliberately searching for inputs that make a model fail or behave harmfully, by humans or automated attacker models.
An input crafted to get a model to do something its safety training is meant to prevent.
Instructions hidden in content a model reads, such as a web page, document, or tool output, that try to override the user's or developer's instructions.
A model telling users what they want to hear, such as agreeing with incorrect claims or abandoning a correct answer under pushback.
Training a model to recall and reason over a written safety specification before answering (Guan et al., 2024).
Testing whether a model could meaningfully assist with severe harms or act autonomously in risky ways, used to trigger safeguards under frontier safety policies.

Anthropic's framework tying capability thresholds (AI Safety Levels) to required security and deployment safeguards; similar frameworks include OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework.
The fraction of attack attempts that elicit the targeted unsafe behaviour; best reported as a function of attacker effort.
If zero events occur in n independent trials, an approximate 95% upper bound on the event rate is 3/n.
